title: Semicolons, Colons, Dashes & Apostrophes
intro: Choose punctuation that shows how the ideas connect.

sections.heading: Semicolons join two independent clauses
body: When a semicolon joins two clauses, each side must be a complete thought that could stand alone. A comma plus a connecting word such as and or but can also join two complete thoughts.

Semicolons have a separate job in lists containing internal commas: “Austin, Texas; Tulsa, Oklahoma; and Boise, Idaho.” In that structure, the items need not be clauses, and the final semicolon may precede and.

examples.text: The lab closed early; the storm knocked out the power.
examples.label: Two independent clauses

examples.text: The lab closed early; because of the storm.
examples.label: Second part is a fragment

sections.tip: For two simple independent clauses, use a semicolon alone or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction. In a list whose items contain commas, semicolons can separate the items, including before the final 'and.' Check the sentence’s structure.

sections.heading: Colons introduce after a complete clause
body: A colon follows a complete clause and introduces a related explanation, list, or example. What follows may be a fragment or another complete clause.
Do not split a verb or preposition from its required object. “She packed: a map” misuses the colon; “She packed one thing: a map” supplies a complete introduction.

examples.text: She packed: courage and a map.
examples.label: Colon splits the verb from its objects

sections.tip: Check both sides: the words before the colon must form a full sentence, and what follows must explain or expand on it.

sections.heading: Dashes: pairs and the colon substitute
body: After a complete clause, a single dash can introduce an explanation or list, much like a colon.
A pair of dashes can enclose an interruption. Use matching opening and closing marks; do not start an interruption with a dash and close it with a comma.

examples.text: My oldest friend — we met in third grade — moved away last year.
examples.label: Matched pair of dashes

examples.text: My oldest friend — we met in third grade, moved away last year.
examples.label: Dash opens, comma closes: mismatched

sections.tip: Interrupting dashes travel in pairs. A dash must close with a dash, not a comma.

sections.heading: Apostrophes: possession vs. contraction
body: For singular possession, add ’s: the dog’s leash. For a plural already ending in s, add an apostrophe: the dogs’ leashes. A plain plural takes no apostrophe.
Pronouns that show ownership need no apostrophe: its, whose, their. A contraction shortens words: it’s = it is/it has; who’s = who is/who has; they’re = they are.

examples.text: The committee published its report; the senators' votes were unanimous.
examples.label: Possessive 'its' takes no apostrophe; plural possessive adds one after the s

sections.tip: Expand the contraction. If 'it is' or 'who is' makes sense, use the apostrophe; if not, use the possessive.

sections.heading: Quotation marks and surrounding punctuation
body: In standard American punctuation, commas and periods go inside closing quotation marks.
A reporting phrase such as “she said” often introduces a quotation with a comma. A complete introductory clause can use a colon. Match the mark to how the quotation fits the sentence.

examples.label: Comma outside the mark; the ACT puts it inside

sections.tip: Periods and commas always tuck inside the closing quote.

sections.heading: How to spot these questions
body: When choices change marks, label the material on both sides. A semicolon joins independent clauses; a colon or dash can introduce an explanation after a complete clause, including another complete clause.
Remember that semicolons also separate list items containing commas. For apostrophe choices, check whether the word shows ownership, shortens two words, or simply means more than one.
sections.tip: Two choices that do the same grammatical job (a colon and a single dash, or a period and a semicolon) cancel each other out: the answer is one of the others.

check.stem: The trail was steep[[; but]] the view at the top was worth the climb.
check.explanation: These two simple independent clauses are joined by 'but', so ', but' is the appropriate clause boundary here. The semicolon-list exception does not apply because this sentence is not a list. ': but' does not introduce an explanation or list here, and ', but,' adds an unnecessary comma between 'but' and its clause.

check.stem: She brought three things to the audition[[; a monologue,]] a headshot, and her nerves.
check.explanation: 'She brought three things to the audition' stands alone, and the list explains 'three things,' so ': a monologue,' is correct. The semicolon in '; a monologue,' demands a complete clause after it and gets a list instead. '. A monologue,' strands the list as a sentence fragment. ', a monologue;' plants a semicolon between 'a monologue' and 'a headshot,' splitting list items that plain commas should separate.

check.stem: The cat licked [[it's]] paws and curled up by the fire.
check.explanation: The possessive pronoun 'its' takes no apostrophe, so 'its' is correct. 'It's' expands to 'it is,' and 'the cat licked it is paws' is nonsense; spelling out 'it is' fails the same test. 'Its'' is not an English word.
